answers.text: Always give back three lines - drop-off time, pallet count, damage noted - in that order, using the same wording each time, like 'Time:', 'Pallets:', 'Damage:'. If the message doesn't mention damage, write 'none noted' rather than leaving it blank.
List each call needing follow-up on its own line with time, customer, topic and outcome, then count those lines to get the total that still need a follow-up call.
The finish time doesn't work - the crew starts at 8am and only needs about six hours, which lands early afternoon on the 22nd itself, not the 23rd as the note says.
118 compared with 96 is closer to a 23% increase, not 20%.
Output 2, since it gives the 940 tickets and 827 closed that the 88% comes from. Output 1 might well be right, but there's no way to confirm it without running the numbers again yourself.
Email 2, since it backs up the ask with the actual volume numbers from the PO log. Email 1 just says 'we'd expect a better rate' without anything behind it.
1. No, that's personal data. 2. Yes, no vendor detail. 3. No, not signed off yet. 4. Yes, it's already public. 5. No, personal again.
The hourly rates and retainer cap are sensitive enough that I wouldn't paste them in directly, and the non-disclosure clause naming both companies makes me want to be careful with the whole document.
Before the reconciliation summary goes out at month-end, I check the reconciled totals against the warehouse system count.

Step 4 is where it becomes final, so that's where I'd put the gate - flagging anything where the invoice and PO don't match within a small tolerance. Step 1, reading the PDF, also carries risk since a bad extraction feeds everything after it.
